sm: Albert Mohler opens the Friday, November 13, 2026 edition of The Briefing by noting the abrupt resignation of Jensen Huang as president and CEO of NVIDIA, following reports of an adulterous affair with a woman believed to have been a Chinese spy. He says the board was meeting as the news broke and promises a closer look next week. He then turns to a Telegraph report that surrogacy applications in the United Kingdom have almost doubled in a decade, rising from 399 in 2016 to 758 in the past year. He describes surrogacy as a product of moral and technological revolutions and says growth is driven largely by same-sex male couples, and he notes that the United States is far less regulated.

Mohler continues on surrogacy, noting that British Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces pressure to recognize intended parents as legal parents from birth, with binding agreements and background checks. He argues that making the practice more regulated does not make it moral, and that campaigners say children's interests must come before adults' wishes. He criticizes the idea that the reasons for the increase are unclear, and points out that British rules allow reasonable expenses but ban commercial brokering, while the United States has no such limit. He then begins listener questions with a fifteen-year-old girl from Pennsylvania asking when worship crosses the line from worshiping the true God to a false one, and he stresses that worship must be directed to the one true and living God.

Answering the worship question, Mohler says Christian worship must honor the Triune God of Scripture, in spirit and in truth, with the gospel proclaimed and Christ declared Lord. He calls much charismatic practice dangerous and confusing, oneness Pentecostalism heresy, and says Catholic sacramentalism needs reform. He adds that some churches say nothing wrong but fall short by not saying enough that is right. A Texas listener then asks why Christians should support Israel when Israel rejected Christ. Mohler points to Romans, chapters nine through eleven, saying God is faithful to his covenant promises, Christians are grafted in rather than replacing Israel, and Christians must never hate the Jewish people.

Mohler says Christians are obligated to love and protect the Jewish people but not to endorse every policy of the secular state of Israel, founded in 1948 and 1949. Next, a young man asks whether it matters which person of the Trinity we pray to. Mohler says the New Testament pattern is to pray to the Father, in the Son, by the Spirit, so prayer is a Trinitarian act. In the final question, a Texas woman who attended a medical school commencement is troubled by a revised Hippocratic oath. Mohler says she is not overthinking it, argues that classical versions included opposition to abortion, and says schools change the words because they do not want to say what they do not believe.
